extracted.intended_audience: CityBeat readers and journalists (media consumers and media professionals interested in journalism ethics)
extracted.subtask_description: An opinion/news column critiquing recent media incidents and offering standards for good journalism practice (plagiarism, corrections, FOIA use, conflicts of interest, etc.). It surveys multiple case studies to illustrate ethical and editorial criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding plagiarism / crediting sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use another person's words or ideas verbatim without credit; using a full paragraph from someone else requires attribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Maureen Dowd used an entire paragraph, almost verbatim, from blogger Joshua Marshall without credit. The piece notes that even if ideas are 'picked up' in conversation, 'a whole paragraph verbatim' should not be reused without giving the original author credit. Anti-patterns include minimizing the victim (e.g., refusing to capitalize the other writer's name) and offering implausible explanations rather than clear attribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prompt and transparent corrections
rubrics_metrics.description: When errors are discovered (including unattributed borrowing), correct them quickly online and provide a formal correction in print or equivalent venues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dowd's response: 'we're fixing it on the web, to give josh credit, and will include a note, as well as a formal correction tomorrow.' The piece praises 'Dowd and The Times quickly corrected it,' indicating timeliness and transparency in correction is expected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify and correctly attribute quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: Verify that quoted text is attributed to the correct person; do not republish second‑hand or misattributed quotes without checking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Guardian reportedly misattributed a jokey quote to Joshua Marshall (it originated with another blogger). The article criticizes repeating misattributions and stresses careful verification of who actually said a quoted line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use freedom of information (FOIA) and document digging to hold government accountable
rubrics_metrics.description: Pursue FOIA requests and dig into public records to expose wrongdoing and to factually underpin investigative reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heather Brooke's five-year FOIA campaign forced disclosure of Parliamentary expense accounts; the Daily Telegraph later named names based on those records. Mentors and internships that encourage 'digging up documents' are cited as crucial to this work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grant time and space for interpretive journalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpretive journalism needs editorial support and longer form to explain complex issues so readers understand the implications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author: 'Interpretive journalism can be a joy to read. It takes talent and editors willing to grant the needed time. Yes, the stories are long, but they have to be if the reader is to say, "Oh, now I get it" or "Holy shit!"' Examples: two Enquirer stories praised for meeting those standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local reporting should cover public-health and workplace implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Local news should examine practical implications of public-health issues (e.g., sick days, employer policies) and quote relevant experts such as physicians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The column asks: 'Where are the local stories quoting physicians on the virtues of employees with flu staying home … and getting paid sick days? Or parents being paid to stay home...' It stresses attention to low-paid workers (hospitality/restaurant) most likely to lack paid sick leave.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency about journalists' outside income and conflicts
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists should disclose outside income and media organizations should have clear, enforceable policies to avoid conflicts of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Tom Friedman charged $75,000 for a speech; after scrutiny he returned it. NYTimes ethics guidelines cited allow speaking fees only from certain nonprofit groups. The author discloses his own income sources and calls for greater transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply consistent standards when naming private matters of public officials
rubrics_metrics.description: Name public officials in reporting or reviews when those matters impinge on their public responsibilities; apply the same standard consistently across different personal matters (e.g., sexual orientation vs. other private acts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NPR deleted names from a review that named politicians discussed in a film; critics argue this is inconsistent since media wouldn't hesitate to name officials for other private conduct if relevant. Barney Frank's point supports naming when it is pertinent to public responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Challenge bigotry on-air rather than placating
rubrics_metrics.description: Hosts and moderators should confront racist or bigoted caller statements instead of responding dismissively or placating the speaker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern cited: WDBZ host responded 'Alright, Bernadette, thank you, sis.' after an on-air caller made an explicitly bigoted accusation, rather than challenging the statement. The critique implies hosts bear responsibility to push back.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adhere to employer ethics rules on outside engagements and return inappropriate fees
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow newsroom/employer rules regarding speaking fees and outside engagements; if a fee violates policy, return it and be transparent about the situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tom Friedman returned a $75,000 speaking fee after questions were raised; the NYTimes ethics guideline limiting speaking fees to educational/nonprofit groups is cited as a standard to follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek and publish images from conflicts where possible; note absence where suppressed
rubrics_metrics.description: Strive to obtain visual documentation of conflicts; the absence of images can itself indicate government suppression and is newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The column notes a striking lack of images from Sri Lanka's civil war and states that Sri Lanka 'reminds us of what an authoritarian government can achieve when it decides it doesn’t want something reported,' implying reporters should both try to get images and report on their absence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be measured before accusing intentional wrongdoing (plagiarism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid rushing to label instances as intentional plagiarism without examining mechanics and motives; consider whether corrections and context mitigate intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Joshua Marshall's response: 'I generally think we’re too quick to pull the trigger with charges of plagiarism... Whatever the mechanics of how it happened, I never thought it was intentional.' The article uses this to caution sensational accusations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mentorship and practical training build investigative reporting skills
rubrics_metrics.description: Mentors, internships, and hands-on assignments (e.g., digging documents) are important for developing journalists who can pursue FOIA work and investigative reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heather Brooke credits a city editor, professors, colleagues, and an internship where she covered the Legislature; a former city editor recalled assigning her to 'dig up documents,' which planted the seed for her later investigative work.
